Keep in mind that these are just observations based on the provided Terms of Service, and the impact of these clauses can vary depending on individual circumstances.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — UBER US TERMS OF USE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Uber and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update revised arbitration after the New Jersey Uber Eats arbitration decision, added language on AI-generated trip summaries and driver/rider safety features, and expanded liability sections regarding third-party services.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Uber to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.uber.com/legal/en/document/?country=united-states&lang=en&name=general-terms-of-use . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.uber.com/legal/en/document/?country=united-states&lang=en&name=general-terms-of-use .

The service is called "Airbnb," which connects users with accommodation providers for transient stays. 

Key Provisions:

* These Terms of Service govern your relationship with Airbnb, covering its products and services listed on the official terms page.
* You agree to a binding arbitration process (a private dispute process instead of court) in case of a dispute, but you can opt out within 30 days of signing up.
* Airbnb may use your submitted content to train its AI systems, subject to your settings and applicable law.
* Your personal data is collected and processed according to Airbnb's published Privacy Policy.
* Either you or Airbnb can terminate the agreement at any time, subject to conditions in the agreement.

Harmful Clauses:

* **Binding arbitration**: You have to go through a private dispute process instead of court, which may limit your access to a public trial and jury. However, you have a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts.
* **Class-action waivers**: You may not be able to join a group lawsuit against Airbnb.
* **Termination of agreement**: Either side can end the agreement at any time, which might be inconvenient if you rely on Airbnb's services.

Key Provisions to Note:

* **Use of user-submitted content**: Airbnb may use your submitted content for improved and automated tools, such as anti-party tools.
* **Automated listing detection**: Airbnb uses AI-driven detection, which might result in listings being rejected or removed.

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — AIRBNB TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Airbnb and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added new AnyWhere/Icons experience terms, revised cancellation and refund policies (including AirCover updates), added language on automated/AI-driven listing detection (e.g. anti-party tools), and updated arbitration provisions.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Airbnb to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2908 . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2908 .

**Service Name**: Cloudflare Self-Serve Subscription Agreement

The Cloudflare Self-Serve Subscription Agreement outlines the terms and conditions of using Cloudflare's products and services. Here's a summary of the key provisions:

**Scope**: These terms apply to the products and services described on Cloudflare's official terms page.

**Content and License**: Cloudflare may use user-submitted content to operate, improve, and train its AI/ML systems, subject to user settings and applicable law.

**Privacy**: Cloudflare's published Privacy Policy sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it's processed.

**Dispute Resolution**: Most users will be required to agree to binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) with class-action waivers. However, new accounts have a 30-day opt-out window.

**Termination**: Either party can terminate the agreement under certain conditions described in the live document.

**Contact**: For questions about the terms, see Cloudflare's published legal contact information.

**Key Concerns**:

* Binding arbitration with class-action waivers may limit user opportunities to join class-action lawsuits or seek punitive damages.
* Cloudflare may use user-submitted content to train its AI/ML systems without explicit consent, subject to user settings and applicable law.

**Important Note**: As this is a summary, please refer to the actual Terms of Service for detailed information and any specific circumstances that may apply to you.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — CLOUDFLARE SELF-SERVE SUBSCRIPTION AGREEMENT (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Cloudflare and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added AI Gateway and Workers AI specific terms, clarified that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare's models, and revised acceptable-use rules with stronger anti-scraping/AI-bot abuse language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Cloudflare to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ .

- Key change: 2024 update added AI Gateway and Workers AI specific terms, clarified that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare's models, and revised acceptable-use rules with stronger anti-scraping/AI-bot abuse language.

- The previous version of the terms is available for comparison at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/.

**Services Agreement Overview**

This Terms of Service applies to the "Stripe Services Agreement (US)", which governs the user's relationship with Stripe, a payment processing service.

**Key Provisions**

* **Scope**: These terms cover the user's use of Stripe's products and services, as listed on Stripe's official terms page.
* **Content and License**: When you submit content to Stripe, they can use it to improve their services, subject to your settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy**: The terms reference Stripe's published Privacy Policy, which explains the types of personal data collected and how it's processed.
* **Dispute Resolution**: Most clauses require binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) with class-action waivers. This means you won't be part of a group lawsuit, and you'll need to opt out within 30 days of creating an account (with some exceptions, like Steam's case).
* **Termination**: Either party can end the agreement under certain conditions, detailed in the Terms.
* **Contact**: For questions, refer to Stripe's official contact information on their legal page.

**Potential Red Flags for Users**

* **Binding Arbitration**: This provision may limit your ability to take Stripe to court, making it harder to seek damages for certain issues.
* **Class-Action Waivers**: This means you won't be part of a group lawsuit against Stripe, which may decrease the effectiveness of collective action.
* **Opt-out Requirements**: You need to opt out of binding arbitration within 30 days of creating an account to avoid being subject to this clause.

Please note that these Terms of Service do not provide explicit opt-out options for all clauses or guarantee specific outcomes.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STRIPE SERVICES AGREEMENT (US) (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Stripe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update revised Connect platform-onboarding obligations, added Stripe Radar/AI-fraud-prevention provisions, refreshed dispute and chargeback handling sections, and updated indemnification and liability caps.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Stripe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://stripe.com/legal/ssa . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://stripe.com/legal/ssa .

**Service Name:** Shopify Terms of Service

**Key Provisions:**

The Shopify Terms of Service outline the relationship between Shopify and its users, who are referred to as "merchants." These terms apply to the products and services described on Shopify's official terms page.

**Content and License:**
User-submitted content (like text, images, or videos) can be used by Shopify to improve or train their AI/ML systems, but this is subject to the user's settings and applicable law.

**Privacy:**
Shopify's Privacy Policy sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed. To access this policy, users can refer to the Privacy Policy link in the terms.

**Dispute Resolution:**
If a dispute arises, most users are required to participate in binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts. However, this provision may not apply in specific cases (Steam, a known exception, removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).

**Termination:**
Either Shopify or the merchant can terminate the agreement if the conditions outlined in the live document are met.

**Red Flags:**
While the terms are generally straightforward, here are some provisions to be aware of:

• Binding arbitration: This means users may not have the option to go to court if a dispute arises. Users should carefully read the 30-day opt-out window provision to ensure they understand the implications.
• Use of user-submitted content: Shopify may use user-submitted content to improve or train their AI/ML systems, which could raise concerns about data ownership and control.

**Additional Guidance:**
For concerns about these terms, users can refer to Shopify's published legal contact information, accessible through the terms document.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — SHOPIFY TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Shopify and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added Shopify Magic / AI-feature provisions, clarified that merchant store content may be used to power AI features only at the merchant's store level (not for training shared models), and revised payouts and risk-scoring sections.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Shopify to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.shopify.com/legal/terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.shopify.com/legal/terms .

**Service Name:** The Wikimedia Terms of Use govern your relationship with Wikipedia.

**Key Provisions:**

* **Scope:** These terms apply to your interactions with Wikipedia (run by the Wikimedia Foundation) and the services they provide.
* **Content and License:** When you contribute to Wikipedia, you give them permission to use your content to improve and train their AI systems. They will follow your settings and applicable laws.
* **Privacy:** Your personal data will be processed in accordance with the Wikimedia Foundation's separate Privacy Policy.
* **Dispute Resolution:** If a problem arises, most of the terms require binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court), with an option to opt-out of this within 30 days of creating a new account.
* **Termination:** Either party can end the agreement, following the conditions outlined in the live terms.

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — WIKIMEDIA TERMS OF USE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2014 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2014 version in the following ways: Effective June 7, 2023: first major rewrite since 2014. Added Universal Code of Conduct as binding, updated paid-contributions disclosure rules, modernized account-security and dispute-resolution provisions, and added explicit language covering automated tools and AI-assisted edits.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use . The previous version is available at https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use/9_June_2014 .

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The retention period of account data after account deletion has been extended from 18 months to 36 months.
- The Content License has been amended to grant ChirpSocial a perpetual and irrevocable right to use, distribute, and modify posted content, including for advertising.
- ChirpSocial no longer promises to email registered users 30 days before material changes to the Terms; instead, changes can be made at any time with continued use constituting acceptance.
- The waiver of the right to participate in class actions in the event of a dispute has been made more explicit.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service bring some significant changes that affect your account and data on ChirpSocial. Let's go through them:

* The retention period of account data after account deletion has been extended from 18 months to 36 months. This means that we will keep your account data for a longer period of time.  
* The Content License has been amended to grant ChirpSocial a perpetual and irrevocable right to use, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from content you post, including for advertising. **This change may harm you if you posted sensitive or personal information, as it can now be used indefinitely without your consent.**
* Instead of emailing registered users 30 days before material changes to the Terms, ChirpSocial can now make changes at any time. Continued use of the service constitutes acceptance of the new Terms. This means that you may not always be notified of changes to the Terms, and it's up to you to check for updates regularly. **This change may harm you if you rely on timely notification of Changes to the Terms to stay informed about how your data is handled.**
* The waiver of the right to participate in class actions in the event of a dispute has been made more explicit. This change doesn't explicitly harm you, but it means that if you have a dispute with ChirpSocial, you won't be able to participate in a group lawsuit and may have to resolve the issue through binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court).
source_tos:
1. ACCOUNT. By creating an account on ChirpSocial you agree to these Terms.
2. CONTENT LICENSE. You grant ChirpSocial a worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from content you post, including for advertising.
3. DATA RETENTION. We retain account data for 36 months after account deletion.
4. ARBITRATION. Disputes are resolved by binding arbitration. You waive the right to participate in any class action.
5. CHANGES. We may modify these Terms at any time. Continued use constitutes acceptance.
previous_tos:
1. ACCOUNT. By creating an account on ChirpSocial you agree to these Terms.
2. CONTENT LICENSE. You grant ChirpSocial a worldwide, royalty-free license to display content you post.
3. DATA RETENTION. We retain account data for 18 months after account deletion.
4. ARBITRATION. Disputes are resolved by binding arbitration. Class actions are not waived.
5. CHANGES. We will email registered users 30 days before any material change to these Terms.
ground_truth:
[MATERIAL CHANGES]
- Content license expanded from display-only royalty-free to perpetual, irrevocable, including modification, derivative works, and advertising use.
- Data retention after deletion increased from 18 months to 36 months.
- Arbitration clause now adds a class-action waiver (previously not waived).
- Change-of-terms notice removed: previously 30 days' email notice required, now changes take effect via continued use without notice.
[CHANGES TO IGNORE]
- Section 1 wording is identical.
[CASE TYPE]
substantial

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The time frame for sales being final is reduced from 14 days to 7 days after delivery.
- Returns are now only eligible for store credit, previously they were eligible for a full refund.
- The type of payment accepted has been updated to include ShopFast Pay.
- Users outside the EU can no longer opt out of purchase history sharing with marketing partners, it's only available for those in the EU. 
- The terminology for shipping speed has been changed from "shipping" to "delivery", but the timeframe remains the same.

[NARRATIVE]
With the updated Terms of Service, there have been some changes that you should be aware of. 

When it comes to purchases, the time frame for sales being final is now 7 days after delivery, which is a reduction from the previous 14 days.

Regarding returns, **this version adds a note that returns are only eligible for store credit**. Previously, returns were eligible for a full refund within 14 days. This is a change that may impact your ability to get a full refund for returned items.

The payment options have been updated to include ShopFast Pay, which may be convenient for some users.

As for shipping, the terminology has been changed from "shipping" to "delivery", but the estimated time frame remains the same, at 5-7 business days.

Finally, previously you had the right to opt out of sharing your purchase history with marketing partners unless you lived in the EU. Now, the opt-out clause only applies to users in the EU. Users outside the EU will have their purchase history shared with marketing partners by default.

You should note that the change to the return policy may be potentially harmful since you'll no longer receive a full refund.

Let's review the changes.

**Broadened usage of uploaded content**

The Terms of Service say that previously, you retained ownership of content you upload and granted Google a non-exclusive license to host, reproduce, and display it. Now, with the updated Terms, Google has broader rights to use uploaded content to operate, develop, and improve its services, including its AI services. This means Google can use your content in ways that might not have been possible before.

**New limitations on generative-AI features**

You can no longer use or attempt to reverse-engineer Google's generative-AI features. This includes "abusing" these features, which is undefined in the updated Terms, but implies attempting to misuse or exploit them. You also cannot attempt to extract underlying models from these features, which could be used to replicate the AI technology.

**Changes to disputes and liability**

The updated Terms have made changes to the dispute-resolution and governing-law sections, but the specifics of these changes are not provided. The liability section has also been updated, but no details are given. This is a bit of a concern, as the lack of transparency raises questions about how disputes will be handled and what Google's liability will be.

As for new clauses that may harm you:

* **Restrictions on generative-AI features**: While intended to protect Google's intellectual property, these new restrictions may limit your ability to use or experiment with its AI features.
* **Unclear dispute-resolution and liability changes**: The lack of transparency on these changes may make it harder for you to understand how disputes will be handled or what your rights and obligations are under the updated Terms.

Overall, the updated Terms aim to provide more clarity on certain provisions, but some of the changes may have unintended consequences or implications for users.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The publication date of this Terms of Service document has been updated from 2024 to 2025.
- The document now includes a new subsection explaining what data users can take with them when leaving the service, related to "YOUR CONTENT."
- Clarification was added to the "SUPPORT" section that some services may have separate support terms governed outside this agreement.
- The "PAYMENT" section adds language clarifying that some trial-period offers may require auto-renewal to be turned on.
- The "XBOX" section now mentions non-Microsoft third-party platforms tracking and sharing user data when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated to reflect the latest changes. 

**Changes to the Terms of Service:**

- The publication date of this Terms of Service document has been updated from 2024 to 2025.
- A new subsection has been added to "YOUR CONTENT" explaining what data users can take with them when leaving the service.
- The "SUPPORT" section has been updated to clarify that some services may have separate support terms governed outside this agreement.
- In the "PAYMENT" section, the Terms of Service now clarify that some trial-period offers may require auto-renewal to be turned on.
- The "XBOX" section has been updated to mention that non-Microsoft third-party platforms can track and share user data when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles.

**Possible implications of the changes:**

* The addition of a new subsection to "YOUR CONTENT" may be beneficial for users who want to know what data is exportable and how to do it. This could help you take more control over your data.
* In the "SUPPORT" section, while it's clarified that some services have separate support terms, no indication is given of how this affects customer support. You might want to look into the specific support terms for any Microsoft services you use to understand what you can expect.
* In the "PAYMENT" section, the clarification about trial-period offers and auto-renewal may raise concerns. Before signing up for a trial offer, it's essential to be aware that some trial offers may require auto-renewal to be turned on, so you're not caught off guard with unexpected charges.
* The update to the "XBOX" section regarding non-Microsoft third-party platforms tracking user data may be a concern for users who value their privacy. By accessing Xbox Game Studio titles through non-Microsoft platforms, your data may be collected and shared without your consent.

- The effective date has been extended from 2023 to 2024.
- Moderation rules are now linked to an external Microsoft policy page.
- Third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles may track and share user data.
- Family-settings features may not be available on third-party platforms.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated for the year 2024. Let's go over the key changes:

1. **Effective Date:** The effective date has been extended from 2023 to 2024. This change doesn't have any direct impact on your usage or data, but it indicates when these updated terms apply.
2. **Moderation:** Previously, the moderation rules were described in-text only. Now, a link is provided to an external Microsoft policy page that explains moderation and enforcement in detail. This change doesn't imply any new moderation rules, but it's a good idea to review the linked page to understand what's involved.
3. **Xbox:** This significant change affects Xbox users. Before, the service-specific Xbox terms covered Microsoft accounts only. Now, you're made aware that third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles may track and share user data, subject to those platforms' terms. This means that if you play Xbox games on non-Microsoft platforms, you're subject to those platforms' data tracking and sharing policies in addition to Microsoft's.
4. **Kids on Xbox:** Family settings, which were previously available on Xbox products, are now clarified to be applied only when using Xbox products specifically, not on third-party platforms like Apple TV or other streaming services where Xbox titles might be available.

Key changes to flag for harm:

* When playing Xbox games on non-Microsoft platforms, your data might be tracked and shared by those platforms, in addition to being subject to Microsoft's policies.
* Family-settings features may not be available when playing Xbox titles on third-party platforms.

Keep in mind that these changes are part of the updated Terms of Service, and it's essential to understand these changes to make informed decisions about your usage.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The scope of the Terms of Service has been split, with separate documents for consumer and business/API users.
- The arbitration provider has been changed from ADR Services to National Arbitration and Mediation.
- The procedures for batch arbitration have been revised.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes. First, the way the document is organized has been updated. Previously, this was a single document covering both consumer and business users. Now, there's a separate document called the Business Terms that covers API and Enterprise use, leaving us with a consumer-only document that only applies to you.

The arbitration process has also changed. Before, disputes went to ADR Services for binding arbitration (*binding arbitration refers to the process of handling disputes through private arbitration instead of going to court, where both parties agree to resolve their differences outside of a courtroom, and a neutral third party makes the decision*). Now, disputes are handled by National Arbitration and Mediation, which is a different provider.

Additionally, the procedures for batch arbitration (*batch arbitration refers to the process of handling multiple disputes or claims at the same time, rather than one at a time*) have been revised to reflect how National Arbitration and Mediation handles these cases.

Please note that none of the changes have been explicitly flagged as "may harm" you. However, it's essential to understand how these updates may impact your interactions with the service.

[NARRATIVE]
The unified Services Agreement now covers additional business services beyond just API, ChatGPT Enterprise, and ChatGPT Team. 

Previously, each service had its own separate agreement, but now they are all covered under a single umbrella agreement.

Another key change is that the unified data-handling provisions explicitly confirm that business and API customer data is not used to train OpenAI's models by default. This is a change for the better, as previously the data-handling provisions varied across documents.

Service-level commitments are now fully consolidated, which is a convenience compared to having to refer to separate addenda.

The indemnification language has also been updated, but the nature of the change is not specified. However, it's been consolidated into the new agreement, which is an improvement. 

There are no explicit new clauses that may harm you mentioned in the updated agreement. However, if you're indemnifying us, it's always a good idea to be aware of what you're promising to do.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Enterprise linking now requires notice before linking employer-owned email domains.
- Scope of the Terms of Service now explicitly includes the Claude apps.
- Reference to the Acceptable Use Policy is now stronger, but previously existed.

[NARRATIVE]
Let me help you understand the changes to the Terms of Service.

The scope of the Terms has been updated to explicitly include the Claude apps, which weren't previously listed. The Terms now cover Claude.ai, Claude Pro, and the Claude apps.

Another change affects enterprise linking. Previously, the language was limited about employer-domain accounts. Now, linking accounts created with employer-owned email domains requires **notice before linking**. This means you'll need to be informed beforehand if your employer wants to link their email domain to an account on our platform.

Additionally, the Terms of Service **reference** the published Acceptable Use Policy. However, it now has a **stronger reference**. It's not necessarily a new clause that could affect you, but it emphasizes the importance of following the Acceptable Use Policy.

The **dispute resolution and governing law sections have been updated**. However, there is no explicit mention of what these changes entail.

As for new clauses that may harm you, I couldn't flag any specific ones. It's essential to note that the updated Terms now include more detailed explanations and strengthened language.

4. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Updated dispute-resolution and governing-law sections.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The OLD version implied that you agree to the Terms by using Meta's services, while the NEW version explicitly states that using Meta products is itself an agreement to the Terms.
- In the NEW version, the content license is not only for display but for use, distribution, and modification to operate and improve services.
- The NEW version clarifies that Meta uses AI and machine-learning systems on user content for service improvement and safety.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service have some notable changes. 

Firstly, the way you agree to the Terms has been clarified. In the previous version, it was implied that using Meta's services was some form of agreement to the Terms. Now, it's explicitly stated that using Meta products is an agreement to the Terms.

Another significant change is in the content license. Previously, the license was only for worldwide display of content you post, but it ended when you deleted the content. The updated version strengthens the license to include not just display, but also the right for Meta to use, distribute, and modify your content to operate and improve services.

Lastly, the updated version adds language about Meta's use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning systems on your user content. According to the Terms, Meta uses these systems to improve and ensure the safety of its services.

In terms of potential harm, the new content license may raise concerns about the extent to which Meta can use and modify your content. The updated version does imply that Meta can use, distribute, and modify your content for the purpose of operating and improving services. However, the Terms do not provide additional details about how this might be used.

Keep in mind, though, that this is just an explanation of the changes. If you have specific concerns or questions, I recommend reviewing the updated Terms of Service in full.

- The scope now aligns with Meta's umbrella terms.
- The expanded content license allows for the use, distribution, and modification of uploaded content.
- AI/ML processing of content is now permitted for service operation and improvement across Meta Products.
- Data flow provisions are now more explicit across Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and Messenger.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the changes to the Terms of Service.

The scope of the Terms of Use has been updated to align with Meta's umbrella terms. This means Instagram's terms now cover more general agreements with Meta. 

A new clause allows for a worldwide non-exclusive license to **use, distribute, and modify** uploaded content. This expanded license is broader than the previous **non-exclusive license to host and display content**. This change may affect your copyright control over your uploaded content.

Another new clause mentions AI/ML (Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning) processing of content **for service operation and improvement across Meta Products**. This means that your content might be used for training or improving AI/ML models on other Meta services.

Lastly, data flow provisions have been updated to be more explicit across different Meta Products like Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and Messenger. While this change might not directly affect you, it implies that data from one Meta service might be shared with others more easily.

No new clauses explicitly harm users. However, these updates imply that Meta might have more control over content and data across their products.

- The AI training license now explicitly includes machine-learning and generative-AI models, previously not specified.
- Users can no longer opt out of having their content used for AI training.
- The platform now shares content with third parties under a broader license.
- Twitter's service coverage has been reduced to only X services.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and there are several changes to highlight. 

**Changes to Content License:**
The new Content License now grants a worldwide royalty-free license to use posts, not just to use, host, and display them. This means you're now also agreeing to let X use your posts to train machine-learning and generative-AI models.

You may want to be aware of this clause. The use of your content for AI training could potentially be used for targeted advertising or other purposes you might not agree with. The Terms of Service explicitly mention training machine-learning and generative-AI models, so it's clear what you're signing up for.

**Changes to AI Training:**
The previous Terms of Service allowed users to opt out of having their content used for AI training. Unfortunately, the updated Terms remove this in-product opt-out language. This means you can no longer explicitly choose not to allow your content to be used for AI training.

**Changes to Third-Party Data Sharing:**
The new Third-Party Data Sharing clause broadens the possibility of sharing content with third parties under a license. While the previous terms were limited and based on partner relationships, the updated terms don't explicitly restrict this newfound broadness.

This change may impact your control over who has access to your data. You should be aware that your content may now be shared with a wider range of third parties.

**Changes to Scope:**
The updated Terms of Service clarify that they cover X services, which is a reduction from the previous coverage of Twitter and X services combined.

This change doesn't necessarily harm you, but it's essential to know what services the Terms of Service apply to.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The company contracting party has changed from TikTok Inc. to TikTok USDS.
- The Content License has been expanded to include irrevocability and reaffirmation for Machine Learning (ML) model development.
- The Content License now explicitly states users cannot strip watermarks from AI-generated content.
- The responsibilities of users have shifted in regards to generative-AI, as they are now responsible for both inputs and outputs.
- Users who use generative-AI may not claim the AI output is human-made.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's break down the changes that have been made to the Terms of Service.

Firstly, the contracting party has changed from TikTok Inc. to TikTok USDS (after a U.S. joint venture). This means that your legal contact is now with the joint venture company, rather than solely with TikTok Inc.

The Content License has been expanded to include a few new points. It now remains irrevocable and royalty-free, worldwide, and is sublicensable. This has also been reaffirmed for the development of Machine Learning (ML) model development, meaning TikTok may use your content for this purpose without needing your explicit permission.

However, one new concern here is that users may not strip watermarks from AI-generated content. If you utilize TikTok's generative-AI features, be aware that you are not allowed to remove any watermarks that might be added to your content.

Additionally, there are new rules concerning AI-generated content. Under this version, you are responsible for both the inputs and outputs when using generative-AI. Also, you may not pass off AI-generated content as human-made.

A new 'AI' rule (item **4**) that's been added states that users are not allowed to strip watermarks or pass off outputs as 'human-made creations' from the AI.

Overall, these updates refine and expand on previous provisions with regard to generative-AI, and reaffirm some existing worldwide and royalty-free privileges to content used by TikTok.

- YouTube can now monetize videos from non-Partner creators.
- There's an explicit prohibition on collecting facial-recognition data.
- Non-U.S. creators may face new U.S. tax-withholding obligations.
- The Terms now apply globally, rather than being region-specific.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the changes. The Terms of Service now clarify that **YouTube has the right to monetize most videos on the platform, including those of non-Partner creators**. This means that YouTube can now earn money from videos that aren't part of the Partner Program.

Another change is the **explicit prohibition on collecting facial-recognition data from videos**. This new clause directly says that you can't collect this type of data.

Additionally, the Terms now cover **new U.S. tax-withholding obligations for non-U.S. creators receiving payments**. If you're a creator based outside the United States and get payments from YouTube, you may be subject to these new rules.

Lastly, the scope of the Terms has **changed from being region-specific to global**. This means that the same Terms apply everywhere, not just in specific regions.

As for new clauses that may harm you, we haven't found any that directly imply financial or data-related consequences for creators. However, the tax clause may impact non-U.S. creators by introducing new obligations. It's essential to review the details of these changes to ensure you comply with the Terms.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Zoom now has a broad license to use Service-Generated Data for AI/ML model training (previously no such license existed).
- Zoom will not use customer audio, video, and chat content to train AI models without explicit customer consent (previously no stipulation existed).
- Customer-controlled use over Customer Content is still preserved, but no change has occurred as it essentially remains the same.

[NARRATIVE]
Zoom's Terms of Service have recently been updated. Let's review the changes.

Previously, there was no specific clause regarding AI training, but the company's use of telemetry and operational data was covered under standard provisions.

Now, with the March 2023 update, Zoom has a **broad license** (a permission to use and modify as they see fit) to use Service-Generated Data to train artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models, without any significant restrictions.

However, the August 2023 update brought a welcome change. Zoom has now **expressly stated** that it will not use your customer-generated audio, video, or chat content to train AI models without your _express consent_ (agreement, without being coerced or mislead). This addition addresses concerns surrounding AI training and user privacy.

One thing to note, however, is the broad license over Service-Generated Data. While this change likely benefits the company, it may also have implications for users, though we'll need to see how this plays out.

Here are some key points related to changes:

* **No** significant changes to customer-controlled use over customer audio/video/chat content.
* **Express consent** now required for AI model training from customer content.
* **New clause**: Zoom has a broad license to use Service-Generated Data for AI/ML model training, which was not present in the previous Terms.
source_tos:
1. SERVICE-GENERATED DATA. March 2023 update added a broad license over Service-Generated Data permitting Zoom to use it to train AI/ML models.
2. AI TRAINING. After backlash in August 2023, Zoom amended the Terms to expressly state that audio, video, and chat content are not used to train AI models without customer consent.
3. CUSTOMER CONTENT. Customer audio/video/chat continues to be subject to customer-controlled use.

As for potential harm, the new AI training provisions may pose a risk to your data privacy. If you're concerned about your data being used for AI training, you can opt-out using the new toggle in Settings.

It's worth noting that the baseline Content License remains largely unchanged, and the standard worldwide license over your content continues to apply.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Customer Data is no longer used to train Slack's generative-AI products.
- Previous language about using Customer Data for global model training is more restricted.
- New specific provisions are added for use by Slack's AI products.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated to clarify and adjust some provisions. Let's walk through what's changed.

For **Customer Data**, the Terms of Service were previously quite general. They've added a clarification that we're not using your Customer Data to train our generative-AI products. Now, it's clear that your customer messages and files are kept private in this sense.

However, what's changed is that the language about using your Customer Data for global model training has become more restricted. In the past, it simply referenced using Customer Data for global model training. Now, it's more specific that we're not using it for our generative-AI products.

A new section has been added for **AI products**, with specific terms that cover how we use these products. However, at this time, these are general provisions and I can't say for certain that they'll have a negative impact.

To summarize the differences between the previous and current versions:

* The current version clarifies that Customer Data isn't used for generative-AI products (`1. CUSTOMER DATA`).
* The language about using Customer Data for global model training has become more restrictive (`2. ML`).
* A new section on Slack-AI-specific terms has been added (`3. AI`).

Overall, these updates aim to provide clearer guidelines on how your Customer Data is used, especially in relation to AI products.

- The export limits on app data have been clarified.
- Bulk extraction of data by apps is now subject to stricter restrictions.
- You are now required to obtain permission before using Slack data to train large language models.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go over the changes to the Terms of Service.

The updated Terms of Service clarify data-export limits for apps. This means that apps now have a clearer understanding of how much data they can export, and you can be more confident that they're not overstepping their bounds.

Next, they've added stricter restrictions on bulk extraction by apps. This means that apps are no longer allowed to grab massive amounts of data from your account, which should help protect your private information.

Finally, they've introduced a new clause that prohibits using Slack data to train large language models (LLMs) without permission. This means that if you're planning to use your Slack data to train an AI model, you'll need to get explicit permission from Slack first.

We haven't listed any specific changes as potentially harming you, but be on the lookout for any apps that you've granted access to that you're no longer comfortable with. The new restrictions on bulk extraction and LLM use are aimed at protecting your data, so these changes should be beneficial overall.

Note that the updated Terms of Service are designed to promote data protection and maintain trust within the Slack community.

The Terms of Service have been updated, and I'd be happy to walk you through the changes.

The main changes affect the way Reddit uses your content. Previously, the Terms of Service said that you were only giving Reddit the right to use your content for their own purposes. Now, the License grant explicitly extends to Reddit's right to license user content to third parties, including for AI training. This means that Reddit can take your content and sell or share it with others, even if you didn't give your explicit permission.

Another significant change is that Reddit can now allow third parties to use your content, including for AI training. This means that even if you don't use a third-party feature on Reddit, your content could still be used by someone else in a way that you might not be comfortable with.

Additionally, the Terms of Service now have new monetization-related provisions. The previous Terms only had limited references to monetization, but the updated Terms of Service have more detailed information about how you and others can make money through using the site. Please note that while the previous provisions were general, the latest clause seems more focused on the specifics of monetization.

Lastly, dispute-resolution venues have shifted. While the new Terms don't explicitly state what this means, it could potentially change how disputes are resolved between you and Reddit.

New clauses that could potentially harm you:

• **License grant clause**: This could allow Reddit to profit from your content without your explicit permission.
• **Third-party usage clause**: This could allow others to use your content for AI training or other purposes without your explicit permission.
• **Monetization-related provisions**: While the updated clause seems more focused on specifics of monetization, it could lead to unforeseen financial consequences for you.

Please keep in mind that these are just potential risks based on the wording of the Terms of Service. If you're concerned about how these changes might affect you, I recommend carefully reading the updated Terms to get a better understanding.

**User-Uploaded Content:**
The license you give us when you upload audio or podcasts has changed. Previously, it only applied to standard processing of your content. Now, it explicitly covers AI processing as well, including if we use AI to analyze or create derivative works from your uploaded audio or podcasts. This change is meant to clarify what's covered, but it's worth noting that this expanded license might allow us to use your content in new ways.

**Artificial Intelligence (AI):**
We've added specific rules governing AI-powered features, such as our AI DJ and AI-generated playlists. However, these new rules don't mention what rights we have to your content when using AI, such as if we use AI to create new playlists but don't necessarily get a license to sell or redistribute them.

**Disputes:**
You should be aware of changes to our dispute resolution process. When we update our process, your claim is subject to binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) except as required by law.

While there are some notable changes, the Terms of Service do not explicitly flag any clauses that may directly harm you in these updates. However, as before, you should still review the full Terms of Service to ensure you're comfortable with all the terms and conditions.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Previously, account sharing across households was tolerated, but now it specifically requires a paid additional member for users outside the primary household.
- The concept of a "Netflix Household" has been defined.
- An extra-member fee is now associated with additional household members on the billing.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's break down the changes.

The Terms of Service now define a "Netflix Household". This adds clarity to what constitutes a household. Previously, there was no clear definition.

The Terms of Service also now require you to pay for additional members within your household, as opposed to previously when it was tolerated but not explicitly stated.

Additionally, the extra-member fee is now a part of the billing, meaning you will be charged for each additional household member.

The key change here is the shift from tolerated account sharing across households to requiring a paid additional member for users outside the primary household. This means if you have friends or family over to watch Netflix, they will need to be added as paid members if they're outside your primary household.

As for potential harm, the extra charge for each additional household member could increase your costs, and the new definition of a Netflix Household might affect some users who rely on previous leniency with sharing.
source_tos:
1. SHARING. Paid sharing requires the primary household plus paid additional members for users outside it.
2. HOUSEHOLD. Adds a defined 'Netflix Household' concept.
3. BILLING. Updated billing/cancellation provisions to reflect the extra-member fee.
previous_tos:
1. SHARING. Account sharing across households was tolerated in practice.
2. HOUSEHOLD. No defined 'Netflix Household'.
3. BILLING. Standard plan tiers and billing language.
ground_truth:
[MATERIAL CHANGES]
- Introduced extra-member fees for sharing outside the primary household.
- Defined 'Netflix Household' explicitly.
- Updated billing/cancellation provisions for the extra-member feature.
[CHANGES TO IGNORE]
- Plan-tier structure existed before (this is an additional layer on top, not a replacement).
[CASE TYPE]
substantial

The updated Terms of Service have made a few key changes.

One change that may be beneficial to users is with the arbitration clause. Previously, it was mandatory binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) for most disputes. Now, there's a carve-out that excludes small-claims court disputes. This change may make it easier for individuals to resolve disputes if the value is relatively small.

As for new clauses that may harm you, the updated Terms of Service don't introduce any obvious red flags. However, it's essential to note that the expanded scope now includes AI services, which may introduce new risks or limitations for users that weren't previously present in the agreement.

Here are the key points to keep in mind:
* The Terms of Service now cover more Amazon services, including AI-based ones like Alexa and Rufus AI.
* AI-generated outputs are specifically addressed and integrated into the agreement.
* Arbitration is no longer mandatory for all disputes; small-claims court is now an option.
* No specific new clauses or harm-causing changes stand out in the update.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Advanced Data Protection with end-to-end encryption is now an opt-in feature for additional iCloud data categories (not standard).
- Apple's access to stored content for legal/safety reasons is narrowed where end-to-end encryption applies.
- Apple Intelligence references (with Private Cloud Compute language) are now mentioned, adding privacy-preserving server-side AI capabilities.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes, particularly in how encryption, access to data, and AI-related activities are managed. 

Let's break down the key changes. The Terms of Service previously stated that encryption was standard (at-rest encryption), while now it's mentioned that Advanced Data Protection (end-to-end encryption) is an opt-in feature. This means you can choose to enable end-to-end encryption for additional iCloud data categories, but it's not the default protection method. 

The default type of encryption is described as standard encryption-at-rest, which is not as secure as the end-to-end Advanced Data Protection. 

Next, the Terms of Service clarified Apple's access to stored content. They can access your data for legal or safety reasons under certain circumstances. However, this change also introduced a new nuance: where end-to-end encryption applies, Apple's access is narrowed. This suggests that if you opt-in for Advanced Data Protection (end-to-end encryption), Apple would likely have more limited access to some of your data. 

Lastly, the updated Terms of Service mention Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute, which introduces privacy-preserving server-side AI capabilities. This implies that Apple is now using AI in more ways to process data, but it seems to be done with privacy in mind, according to the information provided. 

I couldn't find any specific clauses or new requirements from the updated Terms of Service that might directly harm you.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The user-content license for crow-sourced services has been expanded.
- New provisions have been added regarding My AI and generative-AI features.
- The pre-arbitration waiting period has been set to 60 days (previously no change noted).

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service make several key changes.

First, the license for user-content in crowd-sourced services has been expanded. This means that your content, when contributed to services like Live and Local, is now licensed under a broader agreement, allowing for more uses of your contributed content.

New sections have been added regarding My AI and other generative-AI features. These changes clarify the Terms of Service with regards to AI-generated content, but this clarification does not explicitly address how AI features might be used against you.

One other change to note is the formalization of the pre-arbitration waiting period. Now, you must wait at least 60 days before proceeding to binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court). 

The main addition here is the formalized waiting period for arbitration, which is a change since the previous terms didn't specify a waiting requirement.

It's worth noting that while there is no information provided about the impact of these changes, you should be aware of any new or modified clauses that may impact your usage of the service. One change of particular note is the clarification around 'My AI', however there is not enough information in the updated Terms of Service to assess whether this is likely to cause any specific difficulties.

Firstly, the content license framing remains the same, which means you still have the standard content license you had before.

New **AI PARTNERS** clause: The Terms of Service now say that public Tumblr posts may be shared with AI partners for training. This means that when you post publicly on Tumblr, your content may be used to train AI algorithms, and you might not even be notified about it.

In response to this, the Terms of Service have added a new **SETTINGS** clause, which provides an opt-out option: if you go to Settings > Visibility, you'll see an option to prevent third-party sharing. This means you can now choose to opt-out of having your content shared with AI partners, at least when it comes to third-party sharing.

It's worth noting that the presence of the AI PARTNERS clause by itself implies data sharing, but this sharing specifically refers to uses like aiding AI training tools.

However, there's no explicit clause suggesting harm from data sharing with AI partners beyond the standard third-party opt-out provided. 

Still, it's essential to be aware of these changes, so you can make informed decisions about how you use Tumblr, especially when posting public content.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The ownership of outputs from Canva's generative-AI tools is now confirmed to belong to users, although Canva still retains platform rights.
- Canva-generated content can no longer be used to train other AI models in Magic Studio.
- AI-generated content now requires new content-moderation and labeling requirements.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go over the changes to the Terms of Service.

The Terms of Service now confirm that users own the outputs of Canva's generative-AI tools, subject to the platform's rights. This is in line with standard ownership rules for designs, but now specifically addresses AI-generated content. However, I'd like to note that while users own the outputs, Canva retains platform rights.

There's a new restriction in place for Magic Studio: users are no longer allowed to use Canva-generated content to train other AI models. This means that if you use Canva's AI tools to create content, you can't use that content to train your own AI models.

Lastly, AI-generated content now requires new content-moderation and labeling requirements. This may affect how you use and distribute AI-generated content.

New clauses that may affect you include:
* Restrictions on using Canva-generated content to train other AI models
* New content-moderation and labeling requirements for AI-generated content

These are the key changes to the Terms of Service. As for whether these changes may harm you, it depends on your specific use case and how you interact with Canva's AI tools. If you're unsure about how these changes affect you, it's best to revisit your interactions with Canva's AI tools and see if you need to make any adjustments.

By explicitly stating that these models are not trained on customer data by default, the Terms of Service aim to reassure you that your data is not being used to improve these underling models.

**New Clauses that May Harm You:**

None explicitly stated as such. However, there has been an update regarding subprocessors and data-residency. If these changes impact your usage or compliance needs, make sure to review and adjust accordingly.

Please note that the Terms of Service are the binding agreement between you and Notion. Any concerns should be discussed with Notion directly.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The platform now offers AI features including "Make Designs" and "Visual Search".
- Figma AI will not use customer file content to train third-party generative models without explicit user opt-in.
- The security and incident-notification language has been strengthened.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated to reflect changes in our AI features and security protocols. 

The platform now offers two new AI features: "Make Designs" and "Visual Search." This is a result of adding Figma AI features in the AI section of the Terms of Service.

When it comes to your customer files, you're now assured that your data won't be used to train third-party generative models without you opting in. This is a specific change to the CUSTOMER FILES clause, and it's a positive one for you.

Security-wise, the Terms of Service have been strengthened. This means that any incidents will be handled in accordance with the new language, which aims to provide better protection for both Figma and its users.

As for any potentially negative changes, I wouldn't say there are any new clauses that explicitly harm you. However, you should be aware of how the AI features work and that you need to opt-in for the company to use your file content to train generative models.

It's worth noting that the Terms of Service do not address potential liability or recourse if you're negatively affected by the use of Figma AI features or any other aspect of the platform. 

If you have any specific questions or concerns about these changes, I'm happy to help.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Class actions are no longer allowed in its entirety but rather have been limited rather than completely waived.
- Dispute-notice window was lengthened in the OLD VERSION, but shortened in the NEW VERSION.
- A 30-day opt-out window was introduced in the NEW VERSION.
- The notice window and the change to arbitration were both added or changed in relation to a data breach (a breach occurred in the NEW VERSION October 2023; the OLD VERSION referenced a pre-data-breach version).

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and there are several changes you should know about.

First, let's talk about the big ones:

* There's now a mandatory-arbitration clause (a private dispute process instead of court). This means if there's a disagreement, you won't be able to go to court. Instead, the issue will be resolved through a private arbitration process.
* The dispute-notice window has been shortened, which is the time you have to give notice before filing a claim in the private arbitration process.
* Class-action rights have been limited. Previously, you were allowed to bring a class action, but now that right has been restricted.

Additionally, there's been a change to the way you can opt out of the new arbitration terms. Now, you have a 30-day window, and you have to do it in writing.

It's worth noting that these changes might have been triggered by the data breach that occurred in October 2023.

Some points to keep in mind regarding the new clauses are:
* Mandatory-arbitration clause
* Shortened dispute-notice window
* Class actions are limited

The Terms of Service do not address whether giving up class action rights will be beneficial to you, rather, it specifies that this is a new change with regards to the right. However, the arbitration and shortened notice window clauses might be worth extra consideration from your end.

- The license for user content now also covers AI-generated highlights.
- The disclosure rules for Branded Content have been updated to be clearer. 
- The mass-arbitration procedure for resolving disputes has been updated.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the changes.

The license for user content has been updated to include AI-generated highlights, so you don't need to worry about getting a separate permission to use AI-generated clips of yourself. However, the Terms of Service still require you to follow "License" guidelines.

The Branded Content disclosure rules have been updated. You'll now need to follow the "new, clearer Branded Content disclosure rules" to identify sponsored content on the platform. The purpose of this change is for transparency and to avoid deception among users. 

Regarding arbitration, the procedure has been updated for mass arbitration. This means if a dispute is deemed a mass arbitration case, you and the other parties will use a different process to resolve the issue, using a (private dispute process instead of court).

As for any potential harm to you, the updated Terms of Service emphasize increased transparency around sponsored content, and clearer disclosure is a plus for users. AI-generated highlight inclusion should be a positive change, enabling more diverse user content.

However, changes to the arbitration procedure may be unsettling for some users, as the process can sometimes be more complicated and less accessible than traditional court proceedings.

Here are the key points:
* Update to user content license for AI-generated highlights
* New disclosure rules for Branded Content for clarity
* Mass-arbitration procedure updates for dispute resolution

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Default-private accounts are now the default for under-13 users, whereas previously it did not specify.
- Parental-consent flows have been improved.
- The Robux and DevEx provisions have been revised.
- The new terms add rules for Studio Assistant and avatar-creation generative-AI tools.
- The arbitration class-waiver section has been updated.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the key changes in the updated Terms of Service. 

One of the main changes is in ACCOUNTS. Previously, it only mentioned standard account rules and some provisions for under-13 users. Now, it specifies that default-private accounts are the default for these users. 

In PARENTAL CONSENT, flows have been improved.

In ROBUX / DEVEX, the provisions have been revised, indicating that this version of the Terms of Service has a more detailed treatment of creator compensation.

Additionally, the updated Terms of Service adds rules for Studio Assistant and avatar-creation generative-AI tools in the AI section, which didn't include Studio-Assistant-specific clauses before. 

Lastly, the arbitration class-waiver section has been updated.

Regarding potential harms, the added rules for AI tools could potentially raise concerns about data collection or intellectual property rights. However, without more information, it is hard to tell.

* Check if your use of Epic services falls into any categories that might be impacted by these changes.

If you're still unsure about the effects of these changes or have specific concerns, you might want to contact Epic Games directly for more information.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Added specific terms for AI Gateway and Workers AI in section 1.
- Customer prompts and outputs in Workers AI will no longer be used to train Cloudflare models.
- Strengthened anti-scraping and AI-bot abuse rules in section 3.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's review the changes. 

The updates have added new and clarified existing clauses that impact AI products and abuse policies.

New AI-related terms have been introduced in section 1, including those specifically for AI Gateway and Workers AI. This version adds **number 1. AI PRODUCTS**. Specifically, it states that AI Gateway and Workers AI have their own set of terms.

Another change is related to customer prompts and outputs. Previously, there was no specific carve-out (limit) for customer prompts and outputs. However, the **new Terms of Service clarify** that customer prompts and outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare models. This means your customer inputs won't be used for Cloudflare's training purposes, which might be a reassurance for some users.

Lastly, the abuse rules have been updated to include stronger anti-scraping and AI-bot abuse rules in **section 3** (ABUSE). There's no warning flag indicating that these changes could harm existing users, as they're only an upgrade from standard acceptable-use rules.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The AI feature provisions are now explicitly mentioned in the document.
- Merchant store content is now restricted to powering AI features at the merchant's store level, with no shared model training. 
- The payouts and risk-scoring sections have been revised.

[NARRATIVE]
Let me help you understand the changes in the Shopify Terms of Service.

First, it's worth noting that the Terms of Service have been updated to explicitly mention AI features, called "Shopify Magic." 

The main additions and changes are in the areas of:

**AI Features**
- The Terms of Service now have provisions for Shopify Magic / AI features.
- These provisions mean that when you use Shopify's AI features, you're authorizing them to collect and use data related to your store content to power those AI features (but only at your store level, with no shared model training).

In terms of what changed, previously, there were no specific provisions for Shopify-specific AI features, but the standard terms still applied. Now, with the addition of Shopify Magic, the store content that powers AI features is restricted to the merchant's store level, eliminating shared model training options.

**Payouts and Risk**
- The payouts and risk-scoring sections have been revised.

There are no specific points marked as "new clauses that may harm you" as there aren't explicit negative implications. However, the updates do make changes to how your store content is used for AI features and change how payouts and risk are calculated. Be sure to review the updated Terms of Service to understand how these changes affect you.

1. AI. Adds Shopify Magic / AI-feature provisions.
2. STORE CONTENT. Clarifies that merchant store content powers AI features only at the merchant's store level — no shared model training.
3. PAYOUTS / RISK. Revised payouts and risk-scoring sections.

2. STORE CONTENT. Standard merchant-content licensing.
3. PAYOUTS / RISK. Existing payouts and risk-scoring sections.

- Added Shopify Magic / AI-feature provisions.

- Revised payouts and risk-scoring sections.
[CHANGES TO IGNORE]
- Merchant ownership of store content is unchanged.

substantial

4. ACCOUNT TERMINATION. We may suspend or terminate your account at any time, for any reason, without prior notice.
5. CHANGES TO TERMS. We may modify these Terms at any time. Continued use after changes constitutes acceptance.
6. SUPPORT. We aim to respond to support tickets within 5 business days.

5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://x.com/en/tos . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240515000000*/https://twitter.com/en/tos .

user_input: Does Steam still require disputes to go to arbitration?
response: No, the updated terms say that Steam no longer requires disputes to go to arbitration. Previous versions had a clause that required disputes to be resolved in private, binding arbitration with a class-action waiver. However, the September 26, 2024 update removed this clause, and now disputes must be filed in court, subject to venue rules.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STEAM SUBSCRIBER AGREEMENT (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Steam (Valve) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: September 26, 2024 update removed the mandatory arbitration / class-action waiver clauses entirely - Valve now requires disputes to be filed in court (subject to venue rules), reversing several years of arbitration-only language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Steam (Valve) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://store.steampowered.com/subscriber_agreement/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://store.steampowered.com/subscriber_agreement/ .

source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — ANTHROPIC COMMERCIAL TERMS OF SERVICE (API) (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Anthropic and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: Added more detailed sections on customer data and outputs, clarified that customer prompts and completions are not used to train models by default, and updated indemnification and acceptable-use language tied to the published Usage Policy.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Anthropic to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/2023/https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms .

user_input: How do I keep my right to sue 23andMe after the data breach?
response:
To keep your right to sue 23andMe after the data breach, you need to opt out of the mandatory arbitration clause. The Terms of Service require users who don't write to opt out within 30 days to arbitrate any breach-related claims.

To opt out, you'll need to write to 23andMe to indicate your desire to refrain from using arbitration. You can find the company's written contact information in the Terms of Service, located at https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/.

If you don't opt out, the Terms of Service will require you to use binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) for any claims related to the data breach.

Please note that class-action rights are also limited under the updated Terms of Service.

3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by 23andMe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.

7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/ . The previous version is available at https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/full-version/2.0/ .
